In a class of 40 students, 22 play tennis (T) and 18 play hockey (H).

parts.t: Find the number of students who play neither tennis nor hockey.

Find the probability that this student plays exactly one of the two sports.

sols: 22 − 7 = 15 play only tennis and 18 − 7 = 11 play only hockey
Exactly one sport means only tennis or only hockey: 15 + 11 = 26
ms:
M1 for 15 + 11 (= 26) seen as the numerator
A1
oe, e.g. 26⁄40, 0.65

items.stem:
A bag contains 5 red counters and 3 yellow counters.
Cara takes a counter at random, records its colour and puts it back in the bag.
She then takes a second counter at random.
The tree diagram shows some of this information.

parts.t: Complete the tree diagram by writing the missing probabilities on the branches.
Find the probability that both counters are red.

sols: There are 8 counters altogether, so P(red) = <sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> and P(yellow) = <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub>.
The counter is replaced, so the bag is the same for the second pick.
First pick: 3⁄8 on the yellow branch. Second pick: 5⁄8 on each red branch and 3⁄8 on each yellow branch.
Check: each pair of branches adds up to <sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> + <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> = 1 ✓
Follow the red branch, then the red branch again, and multiply.
multiply along the branches of a tree diagram
ms: <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> on the first yellow branch; <sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub>, <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> on each pair of second branches

B2 for all five missing probabilities correct
B1 for the second-pick branches correct, or for 3⁄8 on the first yellow branch

A packet contains 4 orange sweets and 3 lemon sweets.
Idris takes two sweets at random from the packet, without replacement.
The tree diagram shows the probabilities.

parts.t: Find the probability that both sweets are orange.

sols: Only 6 sweets are left and 3 of them are orange, so the second probability is <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>6</sub>.
Different flavours happens two ways: orange then lemon, or lemon then orange.
add the probabilities of the separate routes

items.stem:
Leila plays two games of chess.
The probability that she wins the first game is 0.6.
If she wins a game, the probability that she wins the next game is 0.7.
If she loses a game, the probability that she wins the next game is 0.4.
The tree diagram shows this information.

parts.t: Find the probability that Leila wins both games.
Find the probability that Leila wins exactly one of the two games.
Find the probability that Leila wins at least one of the two games.

sols: Exactly one win happens two ways: win then lose, or lose then win.
‘at least one’ is the complement of ‘none’

items.stem:
A bag contains n red balls and 4 blue balls.
Two balls are taken at random from the bag, without replacement.
The probability that both balls are red is 1⁄3.

parts.t: Show that n² − 5n − 6 = 0.
Solve the equation n² − 5n − 6 = 0 to find the number of red balls in the bag.
Find the probability that both balls are blue.

sols: There are n + 4 balls altogether, so P(first is red) = n⁄n + 4.
After a red ball is removed, n − 1 red balls remain out of n + 3, so P(second is red) = n − 1⁄n + 3.
collect all terms on one side
two numbers with product −6 and sum −5 are −6 and +1
A number of balls cannot be negative, so n = 6
The bag holds 6 red and 4 blue balls, 10 in total.
ms:
M1 for n⁄n + 4 × n − 1⁄n + 3 oe
M1 for 3n(n − 1) = (n + 4)(n + 3) oe
A1 for correct expansion and simplification to the given answer, nfww

M1 for (n − 6)(n + 1) oe, or correct use of the quadratic formula
A1
cao (−1 must be rejected)
